 Latest news Social Security recipients will receive a 3.6% boost to their benefits in January, but “seniors will find themselves disappointed,” warns advocacy group.
 Kevin Dietsch Shannon Benton, director of The Senior Citizens League: “Another year, another COLA that falls short”
 Greg Heilman Update: Oct 22nd, 2026 09:17 EDT Share Make us preferred on Google Inflation jumped once again in the United States in September which resulted in the Social Security Administration’s cost-of-living adjustment (COLA) increase to come in slightly higher than projections prior to its announcement on 14 October . It was the highest COLA since the 8.7% that was applied to benefits in 2023 following a year of rapidly rising prices in the wake of the covid-19 pandemic. 
 Beneficiaries will receive a 3.6% boost to their monthly payments starting in January 2027 . That will translate into a roughly $75 increase on the current average retirement benefit of $2,088.79. 
 However, The Senior Citizens League (TSCL) executive director Shannon Benton says that “seniors will find themselves disappointed.” 
 “Another year, another COLA that falls short of expectations”
 Benton pointed out in a press release on the 2027 COLA that inflation does not occur at one arbitrary point in the year , but “spikes due to a geopolitical event like the Iran war,” and when that happens “seniors pay the price.”
 “Prices go up today, but benefits stay the same for months due to an outdated COLA methodology,” she added. “Working people can request a raise or seek a higher-paying position, but seniors have to make lifestyle cuts or drain their savings until the next COLA.”
 The head of the seniors advocacy group acknowledges that Congress cannot control price swings resulting from shocks in the global economy, “but it can act to ensure that the COLA formula does not leave people behind.” 
 One of the Proposals that Benton has put forth previously include instituting COLAs as often as 12 times a year , to ensure Social Security recipients’ payments remain constantly in step with rises in prices. “We need to consider COLAs that compound quarterly or monthly so seniors can keep up throughout the year when inflation comes in above Federal Reserve targets, like in 2026,” Benton explained .
 “Another year, another COLA that falls short of expectations,” she summed up.
